site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13472:          text: "Start from a recent-June base rate around 90 billion. site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2155:  "child-poverty-2026-given-ctc-3000-refundable": [
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2158:        "child-poverty-2026-given-ctc-3000-refundable-thesis-analyst-fast-2026-06-27t14-21-25z",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2168:        "A fully refundable $3,000 CTC directly raises SPM resources through refundable tax credits",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2169:        "2021 shows large child-poverty sensitivity to refundable credits, but also included stimulus and larger young-child credits",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2588:          text: "Forecast for 2026 child SPM poverty conditional on a refundable $3,000 CTC",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2592:          text: "The resolver is the Census Bureau first print for the Supplemental Poverty Measure poverty rate among people under age 18 for calendar year 2026. This is not the official poverty measure: SPM resources include taxes, refundable credits, transfers and noncash benefits, and subtract medical, work, and child-care expenses while adjusting thresholds for housing costs.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2599:            "Fetched 2021 child SPM poverty rate 5.2 percent, 2020 child SPM 9.7 percent, refundable tax credits moving 9.6 million people out of SPM poverty, and stimulus payments moving 8.9 million people out.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2606:            "Fetched 2022 child SPM poverty rate 12.4 percent, up from 5.2 percent in 2021; overall SPM rate 12.4 percent; refundable tax credits moved 6.4 million people out of SPM poverty, down from 9.6 million in 2021.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2631:          text: "Base-rate/reference class: without the 2021 expanded credit and stimulus environment, recent child SPM poverty sits around 12.4 to 13.7 percent. I use 13.4 percent as the current-policy outside-view anchor before adding the conditional $3,000 fully refundable CTC.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2635:          text: "Time-series prior: I do not extrapolate a simple linear trend because the child SPM series has large policy discontinuities from pandemic stimulus, expanded refundable credits, and their expiration; a persistence prior around the recent non-expanded-CTC level is more defensible.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2639:          text: "Policy mechanism: a fully refundable $3,000 CTC would count in SPM tax-credit resources for eligible families and would matter most for children in low-earnings households who receive little or no current-law nonrefundable credit. It should not mechanically recreate the 2021 5.2 percent rate because the 2021 outcome also reflected larger under-age-6 credits, stimulus payments, and pandemic-era safety-net conditions.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2643:          text: "Anchor 13.4 percent. Subtract 4.7 percentage points for the $3,000 fully refundable CTC, smaller than the 7.2 point 2021-to-2022 child SPM reversal because this condition excludes stimulus and the $3,600 young-child amount. Point = 13.4 - 4.7 = 8.7. For the 80% interval, combine about 1.3 points of recent annual child-SPM movement, roughly 1.5-2.0 points of policy-effect uncertainty, and macro/SPM modeling risk, giving an asymmetric judgmental interval of 5.7 to 12.0.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2647:          text: "Counter-consideration: an outcome near 5.7 percent or lower could happen if wage growth is broad, housing and food burdens ease, and refundable-credit take-up is near-complete. An outcome near 12.0 percent or higher could happen if unemployment rises, rent or medical out-of-pocket costs lift SPM needs, or filing and implementation frictions limit receipt among low-income families.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2674:        "SPM includes taxes, refundable credits, SNAP, housing subsidies, work expenses, medical expenses, and geographic housing adjustments",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2675:        "TCJA-style extension avoids a large scheduled child tax credit drop but does not recreate the fully refundable 2021 expansion",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:3152:          text: "Base-rate/reference-class anchor: the relevant prior is not a 2022-2024 child series because the draft evidence did not fetch the 2024 child value. I use 2022 and 2023 child SPM values plus the 2024 overall SPM signal. After the 2021 refundable-credit expansion expired, child SPM returned to low-to-mid teens, with 2021 at 5.2% treated as an exceptional policy year.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:3164:          text: "Policy mechanism: under the condition, a House-style TCJA extension prevents the child credit from falling back toward the pre-TCJA $1,000 structure, which is poverty-reducing versus expiration. But the extension is not the 2021 fully refundable CTC and therefore does much less for the lowest-income children than the ARPA design that produced the 5.2% child SPM rate.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:3168:          text: "Counter-consideration: if the enacted package preserves more SNAP, Medicaid-linked expense protection, or refundable child credit value than assumed, child SPM could fall toward 11%. Conversely, deeper nutrition cuts, weak employment, or high shelter inflation by 2028 could push the first print above 18%.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:3172:          text: "Start with a post-expansion base of 13.0% to 13.3% from 12.4% in 2022, 13.7% in 2023, and the 12.9% overall SPM signal for 2024. Add about 0.4 percentage point for partial-refundable-credit limits versus a stronger anti-poverty design and about 0.5 point for likely transfer and expense headwinds under the House framework by 2028, giving 14.2%. The interval 10.8% to 18.0% allows roughly -3.4 to +3.8 points around the point, wider than the observed 2022-to-2023 child SPM move of 1.3 points because the horizon is four years, the target is conditional on fiscal legislation, and labor, housing, and medical-expense shocks can compound.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:8506:          text: "The resolver is the Census Bureau official poverty measure for calendar year 2025, reported as the percentage of people in poverty in the first Poverty in the United States: 2025 release/Table A-1 from CPS ASEC. This is not the SPM: taxes, refundable credits, SNAP, housing-cost adjustments, work expenses, medical expenses, and geographic threshold adjustments do not define this official-poverty target.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:9999:            "Census reported Social Security moved 28.7 million people out of SPM poverty in 2024 and medical expenses moved more than 7.0 million people into SPM poverty in 2024; these figures matter less directly for children than refundable credits, SNAP, housing, child care, and payroll-tax effects.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10023:          text: "Counter-consideration: upside risk is meaningful if CPS ASEC measured earnings for low-income families disappoint, housing and child care expenses push more families below SPM thresholds, or benefit participation/resource measurement weakens. Downside risk comes from stronger low-wage earnings, lower inflation thresholds, and larger refundable-credit effects than expected.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10031:          text: "Scenario bounds: a low-side case near 11.7 percent would require strong low-income family earnings and favorable refundable-credit or benefit measurement; a high-side case near 15.4 percent would require weak measured earnings plus housing, child care, medical, or work-expense effects that reduce SPM resources. Values outside the interval would likely need either a recession-scale income miss or an unexpectedly large policy/resource effect.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10058:        "SPM includes taxes, refundable credits, noncash transfers, medical expenses, work expenses, and geographic housing-cost adjustments",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10060:        "calendar-year 2027 rate is sensitive to refundable tax-credit law, SNAP and school-meal policy, child-care and medical out-of-pocket costs, and labor-market income",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10434:          text: "The resolver is the Census Bureau's first published SPM poverty rate for people under age 18 for calendar year 2027. This is not the official poverty measure: SPM resources add taxes, refundable credits, and noncash transfers, and subtract necessary expenses including medical and work expenses, with thresholds adjusted for housing tenure and geography.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10466:          text: "Base-rate/reference-class anchor: absent a new 2021-scale refundable-credit expansion, the most relevant outside-view level is the post-expiration 2022-2024 range of 12.4 to 13.8 percent, with more weight on 2023-2024 because SPM thresholds, rent, medical expenses, and benefit take-up had mostly normalized after the pandemic emergency period.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10474:          text: "Policy mechanism: the child SPM rate is unusually exposed to refundable tax credits, SNAP, school meals, housing subsidies, medical expenses, and child-care/work-expense deductions. For 2027, my central case assumes no broad permanent 2021-style child allowance is in force for the full year, so taxes and transfers keep the rate near the post-pandemic plateau rather than returning to 2021's 5.2 percent.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10478:          text: "Counter-consideration: a material labor-market weakening by 2027 or benefit cuts could push the rate above 17 percent, while a large refundable child-credit expansion, unusually strong real wage growth for low-income families, or lower out-of-pocket medical and child-care costs could move it below 12 percent.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13148:        "tariff receipts are elevated but refund implementation adds uncertainty",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13169:          "https://www.wsj.com/livecoverage/stock-market-cpi-inflation-06-10-2026/card/tariff-refunds-equaled-tariff-collections-last-month-5qhm8A4nfvk2eFlKU9kB",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13275:            "Fetched May 2026 Treasury-reported context: customs duties collected were 22 USD billion, refunds were 22 USD billion, fiscal-year net tariff revenue through May was 189 USD billion versus 81 USD billion a year earlier, and the calendar-adjusted deficit was 2 percent or 24 USD billion below the prior year.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13282:            "Fetched June 2025 context reporting Treasury tariff revenue around 27 to 30 USD billion in June 2025, up from 4 USD billion a year earlier, and fiscal-year tariff revenue above 113 USD billion.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13290:          text: "I start with a recent-June base of about (27 + 66) / 2 = 46.5 billion, add roughly 20 billion for higher interest and entitlement outlays, add 10 billion for tariff-refund and policy noise, and round to a 72 billion point. The 80% interval is set wide at -35 to 210 billion to cover a possible June surplus from strong receipts and a 2023-like high-deficit outlier if payment timing or refunds raise outlays.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13294:          text: "Counter-consideration: elevated tariff receipts and June tax collections could produce a small surplus, especially if refunds are not concentrated in June, which is why the lower bound is negative despite the point being a deficit.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13318:        "tariff-refund shock reduces a revenue tailwind",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13439:            "June 2025 receipts were 526.445 billion, outlays were 499.435 billion, and the deficit/surplus was -27.010 billion; FYTD receipts were 4008.146 billion, FYTD outlays were 5345.518 billion, and FYTD deficit was 1337.372 billion.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13446:            "June 2024 receipts were 466.255 billion, outlays were 532.220 billion, and the deficit was 65.965 billion; June 2023 receipts were 418.317 billion, outlays were 646.085 billion, and the deficit was 227.768 billion.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13453:            "June 2022 receipts were 460.761 billion, outlays were 549.603 billion, and the deficit was 88.842 billion; FYTD deficit through June 2022 was 515.067 billion.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13460:            "Reports cited Treasury figures that May 2026 net tariff revenue was 0 billion after 22 billion collected and 22 billion refunded, FYTD net tariff revenue was 189 billion versus 81 billion a year earlier, adjusted FYTD deficit was 2 percent or 24 billion below the prior year, and Treasury's April-June 2026 borrowing estimate was 189 billion.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13468:          text: "Counter-consideration: if June receipts remain strong and tariff revenues are not fully offset by refunds, the deficit could land near the low end or even close to balance; however, June 1, 2026 is a Monday, so the payment-shift suppression visible in 2024 and 2025 should not repeat.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13472:          text: "Start from a recent-June base rate around 90 billion. Add roughly 55 billion for normal June benefit and Medicare/HHS payments not shifted into May, add about 25 billion for higher interest and entitlement growth, and subtract about 15 billion for still-elevated customs/tariff receipts net of refunds: 90 + 55 + 25 - 15 = 155 billion. Set an 80% interval of 20 to 310 billion to cover tax-payment and refund volatility.",

site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2155:  "child-poverty-2026-given-ctc-3000-refundable": [
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2158:        "child-poverty-2026-given-ctc-3000-refundable-thesis-analyst-fast-2026-06-27t14-21-25z",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2168:        "A fully refundable $3,000 CTC directly raises SPM resources through refundable tax credits",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2169:        "2021 shows large child-poverty sensitivity to refundable credits, but also included stimulus and larger young-child credits",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2588:          text: "Forecast for 2026 child SPM poverty conditional on a refundable $3,000 CTC",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2592:          text: "The resolver is the Census Bureau first print for the Supplemental Poverty Measure poverty rate among people under age 18 for calendar year 2026. This is not the official poverty measure: SPM resources include taxes, refundable credits, transfers and noncash benefits, and subtract medical, work, and child-care expenses while adjusting thresholds for housing costs.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2599:            "Fetched 2021 child SPM poverty rate 5.2 percent, 2020 child SPM 9.7 percent, refundable tax credits moving 9.6 million people out of SPM poverty, and stimulus payments moving 8.9 million people out.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2606:            "Fetched 2022 child SPM poverty rate 12.4 percent, up from 5.2 percent in 2021; overall SPM rate 12.4 percent; refundable tax credits moved 6.4 million people out of SPM poverty, down from 9.6 million in 2021.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2631:          text: "Base-rate/reference class: without the 2021 expanded credit and stimulus environment, recent child SPM poverty sits around 12.4 to 13.7 percent. I use 13.4 percent as the current-policy outside-view anchor before adding the conditional $3,000 fully refundable CTC.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2635:          text: "Time-series prior: I do not extrapolate a simple linear trend because the child SPM series has large policy discontinuities from pandemic stimulus, expanded refundable credits, and their expiration; a persistence prior around the recent non-expanded-CTC level is more defensible.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2639:          text: "Policy mechanism: a fully refundable $3,000 CTC would count in SPM tax-credit resources for eligible families and would matter most for children in low-earnings households who receive little or no current-law nonrefundable credit. It should not mechanically recreate the 2021 5.2 percent rate because the 2021 outcome also reflected larger under-age-6 credits, stimulus payments, and pandemic-era safety-net conditions.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2643:          text: "Anchor 13.4 percent. Subtract 4.7 percentage points for the $3,000 fully refundable CTC, smaller than the 7.2 point 2021-to-2022 child SPM reversal because this condition excludes stimulus and the $3,600 young-child amount. Point = 13.4 - 4.7 = 8.7. For the 80% interval, combine about 1.3 points of recent annual child-SPM movement, roughly 1.5-2.0 points of policy-effect uncertainty, and macro/SPM modeling risk, giving an asymmetric judgmental interval of 5.7 to 12.0.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2647:          text: "Counter-consideration: an outcome near 5.7 percent or lower could happen if wage growth is broad, housing and food burdens ease, and refundable-credit take-up is near-complete. An outcome near 12.0 percent or higher could happen if unemployment rises, rent or medical out-of-pocket costs lift SPM needs, or filing and implementation frictions limit receipt among low-income families.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2674:        "SPM includes taxes, refundable credits, SNAP, housing subsidies, work expenses, medical expenses, and geographic housing adjustments",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2675:        "TCJA-style extension avoids a large scheduled child tax credit drop but does not recreate the fully refundable 2021 expansion",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:3152:          text: "Base-rate/reference-class anchor: the relevant prior is not a 2022-2024 child series because the draft evidence did not fetch the 2024 child value. I use 2022 and 2023 child SPM values plus the 2024 overall SPM signal. After the 2021 refundable-credit expansion expired, child SPM returned to low-to-mid teens, with 2021 at 5.2% treated as an exceptional policy year.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:3164:          text: "Policy mechanism: under the condition, a House-style TCJA extension prevents the child credit from falling back toward the pre-TCJA $1,000 structure, which is poverty-reducing versus expiration. But the extension is not the 2021 fully refundable CTC and therefore does much less for the lowest-income children than the ARPA design that produced the 5.2% child SPM rate.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:3168:          text: "Counter-consideration: if the enacted package preserves more SNAP, Medicaid-linked expense protection, or refundable child credit value than assumed, child SPM could fall toward 11%. Conversely, deeper nutrition cuts, weak employment, or high shelter inflation by 2028 could push the first print above 18%.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:3172:          text: "Start with a post-expansion base of 13.0% to 13.3% from 12.4% in 2022, 13.7% in 2023, and the 12.9% overall SPM signal for 2024. Add about 0.4 percentage point for partial-refundable-credit limits versus a stronger anti-poverty design and about 0.5 point for likely transfer and expense headwinds under the House framework by 2028, giving 14.2%. The interval 10.8% to 18.0% allows roughly -3.4 to +3.8 points around the point, wider than the observed 2022-to-2023 child SPM move of 1.3 points because the horizon is four years, the target is conditional on fiscal legislation, and labor, housing, and medical-expense shocks can compound.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:8506:          text: "The resolver is the Census Bureau official poverty measure for calendar year 2025, reported as the percentage of people in poverty in the first Poverty in the United States: 2025 release/Table A-1 from CPS ASEC. This is not the SPM: taxes, refundable credits, SNAP, housing-cost adjustments, work expenses, medical expenses, and geographic threshold adjustments do not define this official-poverty target.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:9999:            "Census reported Social Security moved 28.7 million people out of SPM poverty in 2024 and medical expenses moved more than 7.0 million people into SPM poverty in 2024; these figures matter less directly for children than refundable credits, SNAP, housing, child care, and payroll-tax effects.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10023:          text: "Counter-consideration: upside risk is meaningful if CPS ASEC measured earnings for low-income families disappoint, housing and child care expenses push more families below SPM thresholds, or benefit participation/resource measurement weakens. Downside risk comes from stronger low-wage earnings, lower inflation thresholds, and larger refundable-credit effects than expected.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10031:          text: "Scenario bounds: a low-side case near 11.7 percent would require strong low-income family earnings and favorable refundable-credit or benefit measurement; a high-side case near 15.4 percent would require weak measured earnings plus housing, child care, medical, or work-expense effects that reduce SPM resources. Values outside the interval would likely need either a recession-scale income miss or an unexpectedly large policy/resource effect.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10058:        "SPM includes taxes, refundable credits, noncash transfers, medical expenses, work expenses, and geographic housing-cost adjustments",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10060:        "calendar-year 2027 rate is sensitive to refundable tax-credit law, SNAP and school-meal policy, child-care and medical out-of-pocket costs, and labor-market income",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10434:          text: "The resolver is the Census Bureau's first published SPM poverty rate for people under age 18 for calendar year 2027. site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10466:          text: "Base-rate/reference-class anchor: absent a new 2021-scale refundable-credit expansion, the most relevant outside-view level is the post-expiration 2022-2024 range of 12.4 to 13.8 percent, with more weight on 2023-2024 because SPM thresholds, rent, medical expenses, and benefit take-up had mostly normalized after the pandemic emergency period.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10474:          text: "Policy mechanism: the child SPM rate is unusually exposed to refundable tax credits, SNAP, school meals, housing subsidies, medical expenses, and child-care/work-expense deductions. For 2027, my central case assumes no broad permanent 2021-style child allowance is in force for the full year, so taxes and transfers keep the rate near the post-pandemic plateau rather than returning to 2021's 5.2 percent.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10478:          text: "Counter-consideration: a material labor-market weakening by 2027 or benefit cuts could push the rate above 17 percent, while a large refundable child-credit expansion, unusually strong real wage growth for low-income families, or lower out-of-pocket medical and child-care costs could move it below 12 percent.",

site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13290:          text: "I start with a recent-June base of about (27 + 66) / 2 = 46.5 billion, add roughly 20 billion for higher interest and entitlement outlays, add 10 billion for tariff-refund and policy noise, and round to a 72 billion point. site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13460:            "Reports cited Treasury figures that May 2026 net tariff revenue was 0 billion after 22 billion collected and 22 billion refunded, FYTD net tariff revenue was 189 billion versus 81 billion a year earlier, adjusted FYTD deficit was 2 percent or 24 billion below the prior year, and Treasury's April-June 2026 borrowing estimate was 189 billion.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13468:          text: "Counter-consideration: if June receipts remain strong and tariff revenues are not fully offset by refunds, the deficit could land near the low end or even close to balance; however, June 1, 2026 is a Monday, so the payment-shift suppression visible in 2024 and 2025 should not repeat.",

site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2155:  "child-poverty-2026-given-ctc-3000-refundable": [
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2158:        "child-poverty-2026-given-ctc-3000-refundable-thesis-analyst-fast-2026-06-27t14-21-25z",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2168:        "A fully refundable $3,000 CTC directly raises SPM resources through refundable tax credits",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2169:        "2021 shows large child-poverty sensitivity to refundable credits, but also included stimulus and larger young-child credits",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2588:          text: "Forecast for 2026 child SPM poverty conditional on a refundable $3,000 CTC",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2592:          text: "The resolver is the Census Bureau first print for the Supplemental Poverty Measure poverty rate among people under age 18 for calendar year 2026. This is not the official poverty measure: SPM resources include taxes, refundable credits, transfers and noncash benefits, and subtract medical, work, and child-care expenses while adjusting thresholds for housing costs.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2599:            "Fetched 2021 child SPM poverty rate 5.2 percent, 2020 child SPM 9.7 percent, refundable tax credits moving 9.6 million people out of SPM poverty, and stimulus payments moving 8.9 million people out.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2606:            "Fetched 2022 child SPM poverty rate 12.4 percent, up from 5.2 percent in 2021; overall SPM rate 12.4 percent; refundable tax credits moved 6.4 million people out of SPM poverty, down from 9.6 million in 2021.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2631:          text: "Base-rate/reference class: without the 2021 expanded credit and stimulus environment, recent child SPM poverty sits around 12.4 to 13.7 percent. I use 13.4 percent as the current-policy outside-view anchor before adding the conditional $3,000 fully refundable CTC.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2635:          text: "Time-series prior: I do not extrapolate a simple linear trend because the child SPM series has large policy discontinuities from pandemic stimulus, expanded refundable credits, and their expiration; a persistence prior around the recent non-expanded-CTC level is more defensible.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2639:          text: "Policy mechanism: a fully refundable $3,000 CTC would count in SPM tax-credit resources for eligible families and would matter most for children in low-earnings households who receive little or no current-law nonrefundable credit. It should not mechanically recreate the 2021 5.2 percent rate because the 2021 outcome also reflected larger under-age-6 credits, stimulus payments, and pandemic-era safety-net conditions.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2643:          text: "Anchor 13.4 percent. Subtract 4.7 percentage points for the $3,000 fully refundable CTC, smaller than the 7.2 point 2021-to-2022 child SPM reversal because this condition excludes stimulus and the $3,600 young-child amount. Point = 13.4 - 4.7 = 8.7. For the 80% interval, combine about 1.3 points of recent annual child-SPM movement, roughly 1.5-2.0 points of policy-effect uncertainty, and macro/SPM modeling risk, giving an asymmetric judgmental interval of 5.7 to 12.0.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2647:          text: "Counter-consideration: an outcome near 5.7 percent or lower could happen if wage growth is broad, housing and food burdens ease, and refundable-credit take-up is near-complete. An outcome near 12.0 percent or higher could happen if unemployment rises, rent or medical out-of-pocket costs lift SPM needs, or filing and implementation frictions limit receipt among low-income families.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2674:        "SPM includes taxes, refundable credits, SNAP, housing subsidies, work expenses, medical expenses, and geographic housing adjustments",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2675:        "TCJA-style extension avoids a large scheduled child tax credit drop but does not recreate the fully refundable 2021 expansion",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:3152:          text: "Base-rate/reference-class anchor: the relevant prior is not a 2022-2024 child series because the draft evidence did not fetch the 2024 child value. I use 2022 and 2023 child SPM values plus the 2024 overall SPM signal. After the 2021 refundable-credit expansion expired, child SPM returned to low-to-mid teens, with 2021 at 5.2% treated as an exceptional policy year.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:3164:          text: "Policy mechanism: under the condition, a House-style TCJA extension prevents the child credit from falling back toward the pre-TCJA $1,000 structure, which is poverty-reducing versus expiration. But the extension is not the 2021 fully refundable CTC and therefore does much less for the lowest-income children than the ARPA design that produced the 5.2% child SPM rate.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:3168:          text: "Counter-consideration: if the enacted package preserves more SNAP, Medicaid-linked expense protection, or refundable child credit value than assumed, child SPM could fall toward 11%. Conversely, deeper nutrition cuts, weak employment, or high shelter inflation by 2028 could push the first print above 18%.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:3172:          text: "Start with a post-expansion base of 13.0% to 13.3% from 12.4% in 2022, 13.7% in 2023, and the 12.9% overall SPM signal for 2024. Add about 0.4 percentage point for partial-refundable-credit limits versus a stronger anti-poverty design and about 0.5 point for likely transfer and expense headwinds under the House framework by 2028, giving 14.2%. The interval 10.8% to 18.0% allows roughly -3.4 to +3.8 points around the point, wider than the observed 2022-to-2023 child SPM move of 1.3 points because the horizon is four years, the target is conditional on fiscal legislation, and labor, housing, and medical-expense shocks can compound.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:8506:          text: "The resolver is the Census Bureau official poverty measure for calendar year 2025, reported as the percentage of people in poverty in the first Poverty in the United States: 2025 release/Table A-1 from CPS ASEC. This is not the SPM: taxes, refundable credits, SNAP, housing-cost adjustments, work expenses, medical expenses, and geographic threshold adjustments do not define this official-poverty target.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:9999:            "Census reported Social Security moved 28.7 million people out of SPM poverty in 2024 and medical expenses moved more than 7.0 million people into SPM poverty in 2024; these figures matter less directly for children than refundable credits, SNAP, housing, child care, and payroll-tax effects.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10023:          text: "Counter-consideration: upside risk is meaningful if CPS ASEC measured earnings for low-income families disappoint, housing and child care expenses push more families below SPM thresholds, or benefit participation/resource measurement weakens. Downside risk comes from stronger low-wage earnings, lower inflation thresholds, and larger refundable-credit effects than expected.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10031:          text: "Scenario bounds: a low-side case near 11.7 percent would require strong low-income family earnings and favorable refundable-credit or benefit measurement; a high-side case near 15.4 percent would require weak measured earnings plus housing, child care, medical, or work-expense effects that reduce SPM resources. Values outside the interval would likely need either a recession-scale income miss or an unexpectedly large policy/resource effect.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10058:        "SPM includes taxes, refundable credits, noncash transfers, medical expenses, work expenses, and geographic housing-cost adjustments",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10060:        "calendar-year 2027 rate is sensitive to refundable tax-credit law, SNAP and school-meal policy, child-care and medical out-of-pocket costs, and labor-market income",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10434:          text: "The resolver is the Census Bureau's first published SPM poverty rate for people under age 18 for calendar year 2027. This is not the official poverty measure: SPM resources add taxes, refundable credits, and noncash transfers, and subtract necessary expenses including medical and work expenses, with thresholds adjusted for housing tenure and geography.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10466:          text: "Base-rate/reference-class anchor: absent a new 2021-scale refundable-credit expansion, the most relevant outside-view level is the post-expiration 2022-2024 range of 12.4 to 13.8 percent, with more weight on 2023-2024 because SPM thresholds, rent, medical expenses, and benefit take-up had mostly normalized after the pandemic emergency period.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10474:          text: "Policy mechanism: the child SPM rate is unusually exposed to refundable tax credits, SNAP, school meals, housing subsidies, medical expenses, and child-care/work-expense deductions. For 2027, my central case assumes no broad permanent 2021-style child allowance is in force for the full year, so taxes and transfers keep the rate near the post-pandemic plateau rather than returning to 2021's 5.2 percent.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10478:          text: "Counter-consideration: a material labor-market weakening by 2027 or benefit cuts could push the rate above 17 percent, while a large refundable child-credit expansion, unusually strong real wage growth for low-income families, or lower out-of-pocket medical and child-care costs could move it below 12 percent.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13148:        "tariff receipts are elevated but refund implementation adds uncertainty",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13169:          "https://www.wsj.com/livecoverage/stock-market-cpi-inflation-06-10-2026/card/tariff-refunds-equaled-tariff-collections-last-month-5qhm8A4nfvk2eFlKU9kB",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13275:            "Fetched May 2026 Treasury-reported context: customs duties collected were 22 USD billion, refunds were 22 USD billion, fiscal-year net tariff revenue through May was 189 USD billion versus 81 USD billion a year earlier, and the calendar-adjusted deficit was 2 percent or 24 USD billion below the prior year.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13282:            "Fetched June 2025 context reporting Treasury tariff revenue around 27 to 30 USD billion in June 2025, up from 4 USD billion a year earlier, and fiscal-year tariff revenue above 113 USD billion.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13290:          text: "I start with a recent-June base of about (27 + 66) / 2 = 46.5 billion, add roughly 20 billion for higher interest and entitlement outlays, add 10 billion for tariff-refund and policy noise, and round to a 72 billion point. The 80% interval is set wide at -35 to 210 billion to cover a possible June surplus from strong receipts and a 2023-like high-deficit outlier if payment timing or refunds raise outlays.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13294:          text: "Counter-consideration: elevated tariff receipts and June tax collections could produce a small surplus, especially if refunds are not concentrated in June, which is why the lower bound is negative despite the point being a deficit.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13318:        "tariff-refund shock reduces a revenue tailwind",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13439:            "June 2025 receipts were 526.445 billion, outlays were 499.435 billion, and the deficit/surplus was -27.010 billion; FYTD receipts were 4008.146 billion, FYTD outlays were 5345.518 billion, and FYTD deficit was 1337.372 billion.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13446:            "June 2024 receipts were 466.255 billion, outlays were 532.220 billion, and the deficit was 65.965 billion; June 2023 receipts were 418.317 billion, outlays were 646.085 billion, and the deficit was 227.768 billion.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13453:            "June 2022 receipts were 460.761 billion, outlays were 549.603 billion, and the deficit was 88.842 billion; FYTD deficit through June 2022 was 515.067 billion.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13460:            "Reports cited Treasury figures that May 2026 net tariff revenue was 0 billion after 22 billion collected and 22 billion refunded, FYTD net tariff revenue was 189 billion versus 81 billion a year earlier, adjusted FYTD deficit was 2 percent or 24 billion below the prior year, and Treasury's April-June 2026 borrowing estimate was 189 billion.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13468:          text: "Counter-consideration: if June receipts remain strong and tariff revenues are not fully offset by refunds, the deficit could land near the low end or even close to balance; however, June 1, 2026 is a Monday, so the payment-shift suppression visible in 2024 and 2025 should not repeat.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:13472:          text: "Start from a recent-June base rate around 90 billion. Add roughly 55 billion for normal June benefit and Medicare/HHS payments not shifted into May, add about 25 billion for higher interest and entitlement growth, and subtract about 15 billion for still-elevated customs/tariff receipts net of refunds: 90 + 55 + 25 - 15 = 155 billion. Set an 80% interval of 20 to 310 billion to cover tax-payment and refund volatility.",

site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2155:  "child-poverty-2026-given-ctc-3000-refundable": [
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2158:        "child-poverty-2026-given-ctc-3000-refundable-thesis-analyst-fast-2026-06-27t14-21-25z",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2168:        "A fully refundable $3,000 CTC directly raises SPM resources through refundable tax credits",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2169:        "2021 shows large child-poverty sensitivity to refundable credits, but also included stimulus and larger young-child credits",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2588:          text: "Forecast for 2026 child SPM poverty conditional on a refundable $3,000 CTC",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2592:          text: "The resolver is the Census Bureau first print for the Supplemental Poverty Measure poverty rate among people under age 18 for calendar year 2026. This is not the official poverty measure: SPM resources include taxes, refundable credits, transfers and noncash benefits, and subtract medical, work, and child-care expenses while adjusting thresholds for housing costs.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2599:            "Fetched 2021 child SPM poverty rate 5.2 percent, 2020 child SPM 9.7 percent, refundable tax credits moving 9.6 million people out of SPM poverty, and stimulus payments moving 8.9 million people out.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2606:            "Fetched 2022 child SPM poverty rate 12.4 percent, up from 5.2 percent in 2021; overall SPM rate 12.4 percent; refundable tax credits moved 6.4 million people out of SPM poverty, down from 9.6 million in 2021.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2631:          text: "Base-rate/reference class: without the 2021 expanded credit and stimulus environment, recent child SPM poverty sits around 12.4 to 13.7 percent. I use 13.4 percent as the current-policy outside-view anchor before adding the conditional $3,000 fully refundable CTC.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2635:          text: "Time-series prior: I do not extrapolate a simple linear trend because the child SPM series has large policy discontinuities from pandemic stimulus, expanded refundable credits, and their expiration; a persistence prior around the recent non-expanded-CTC level is more defensible.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2639:          text: "Policy mechanism: a fully refundable $3,000 CTC would count in SPM tax-credit resources for eligible families and would matter most for children in low-earnings households who receive little or no current-law nonrefundable credit. It should not mechanically recreate the 2021 5.2 percent rate because the 2021 outcome also reflected larger under-age-6 credits, stimulus payments, and pandemic-era safety-net conditions.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2643:          text: "Anchor 13.4 percent. Subtract 4.7 percentage points for the $3,000 fully refundable CTC, smaller than the 7.2 point 2021-to-2022 child SPM reversal because this condition excludes stimulus and the $3,600 young-child amount. Point = 13.4 - 4.7 = 8.7. For the 80% interval, combine about 1.3 points of recent annual child-SPM movement, roughly 1.5-2.0 points of policy-effect uncertainty, and macro/SPM modeling risk, giving an asymmetric judgmental interval of 5.7 to 12.0.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2647:          text: "Counter-consideration: an outcome near 5.7 percent or lower could happen if wage growth is broad, housing and food burdens ease, and refundable-credit take-up is near-complete. An outcome near 12.0 percent or higher could happen if unemployment rises, rent or medical out-of-pocket costs lift SPM needs, or filing and implementation frictions limit receipt among low-income families.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2674:        "SPM includes taxes, refundable credits, SNAP, housing subsidies, work expenses, medical expenses, and geographic housing adjustments",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2675:        "TCJA-style extension avoids a large scheduled child tax credit drop but does not recreate the fully refundable 2021 expansion",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:3152:          text: "Base-rate/reference-class anchor: the relevant prior is not a 2022-2024 child series because the draft evidence did not fetch the 2024 child value. I use 2022 and 2023 child SPM values plus the 2024 overall SPM signal. After the 2021 refundable-credit expansion expired, child SPM returned to low-to-mid teens, with 2021 at 5.2% treated as an exceptional policy year.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:3164:          text: "Policy mechanism: under the condition, a House-style TCJA extension prevents the child credit from falling back toward the pre-TCJA $1,000 structure, which is poverty-reducing versus expiration. But the extension is not the 2021 fully refundable CTC and therefore does much less for the lowest-income children than the ARPA design that produced the 5.2% child SPM rate.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:3168:          text: "Counter-consideration: if the enacted package preserves more SNAP, Medicaid-linked expense protection, or refundable child credit value than assumed, child SPM could fall toward 11%. Conversely, deeper nutrition cuts, weak employment, or high shelter inflation by 2028 could push the first print above 18%.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:3172:          text: "Start with a post-expansion base of 13.0% to 13.3% from 12.4% in 2022, 13.7% in 2023, and the 12.9% overall SPM signal for 2024. Add about 0.4 percentage point for partial-refundable-credit limits versus a stronger anti-poverty design and about 0.5 point for likely transfer and expense headwinds under the House framework by 2028, giving 14.2%. The interval 10.8% to 18.0% allows roughly -3.4 to +3.8 points around the point, wider than the observed 2022-to-2023 child SPM move of 1.3 points because the horizon is four years, the target is conditional on fiscal legislation, and labor, housing, and medical-expense shocks can compound.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:8506:          text: "The resolver is the Census Bureau official poverty measure for calendar year 2025, reported as the percentage of people in poverty in the first Poverty in the United States: 2025 release/Table A-1 from CPS ASEC. This is not the SPM: taxes, refundable credits, SNAP, housing-cost adjustments, work expenses, medical expenses, and geographic threshold adjustments do not define this official-poverty target.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:9999:            "Census reported Social Security moved 28.7 million people out of SPM poverty in 2024 and medical expenses moved more than 7.0 million people into SPM poverty in 2024; these figures matter less directly for children than refundable credits, SNAP, housing, child care, and payroll-tax effects.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10023:          text: "Counter-consideration: upside risk is meaningful if CPS ASEC measured earnings for low-income families disappoint, housing and child care expenses push more families below SPM thresholds, or benefit participation/resource measurement weakens. Downside risk comes from stronger low-wage earnings, lower inflation thresholds, and larger refundable-credit effects than expected.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10031:          text: "Scenario bounds: a low-side case near 11.7 percent would require strong low-income family earnings and favorable refundable-credit or benefit measurement; a high-side case near 15.4 percent would require weak measured earnings plus housing, child care, medical, or work-expense effects that reduce SPM resources. Values outside the interval would likely need either a recession-scale income miss or an unexpectedly large policy/resource effect.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10058:        "SPM includes taxes, refundable credits, noncash transfers, medical expenses, work expenses, and geographic housing-cost adjustments",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10060:        "calendar-year 2027 rate is sensitive to refundable tax-credit law, SNAP and school-meal policy, child-care and medical out-of-pocket costs, and labor-market income",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10434:          text: "The resolver is the Census Bureau's first published SPM poverty rate for people under age 18 for calendar year 2027. This is not the official poverty measure: SPM resources add taxes, refundable credits, and noncash transfers, and subtract necessary expenses including medical and work expenses, with thresholds adjusted for housing tenure and geography.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10466:          text: "Base-rate/reference-class anchor: absent a new 2021-scale refundable-credit expansion, the most relevant outside-view level is the post-expiration 2022-2024 range of 12.4 to 13.8 percent, with more weight on 2023-2024 because SPM thresholds, rent, medical expenses, and benefit take-up had mostly normalized after the pandemic emergency period.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10474:          text: "Policy mechanism: the child SPM rate is unusually exposed to refundable tax credits, SNAP, school meals, housing subsidies, medical expenses, and child-care/work-expense deductions. For 2027, my central case assumes no broad permanent 2021-style child allowance is in force for the full year, so taxes and transfers keep the rate near the post-pandemic plateau rather than returning to 2021's 5.2 percent.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10478:          text: "Counter-consideration: a material labor-market weakening by 2027 or benefit cuts could push the rate above 17 percent, while a large refundable child-credit expansion, unusually strong real wage growth for low-income families, or lower out-of-pocket medical and child-care costs could move it below 12 percent.",
